headline: Peanut Bunker Push Sachuest, Blues Crash the Shoreline While Bass Hold to the Dark
subhead: Midsummer means daytime blues on bunker, night bass on the ledges, and a tog bite that's stubborn until the water cools.
body_markdown:
First thing I noticed hopping out to the ledge below Brenton Point Tuesday morning — peanut bunker, thick as pepper, pinned right against the rock in that first hour of light. Not balled up tight like September stuff, more like a nervous smear along the shoreline, but it's there, and where there's peanut bunker in mid-July, something's usually working it from below. Sure enough, about twenty minutes in, the whole pod erupted about sixty yards off the point — bluefish, and not small ones either. Three, four pound choppers busting through the pod like they were late for something. That's been the story all along the south-facing shore this week, from Sachuest around to Second Beach — bunker schools moving tight to structure, blues working them hard in the mid-morning sun.

Stripers are a different animal right now. Water's warm enough on the surface — comfortable, not cold, low seventies out front of Newport most days — that the bass have pushed their feeding into the dark hours and stayed there. I fished the ledges off Ocean Drive two nights this week on the last two hours of the ebb, working a black Slug-Go and a bone Danny plug, and connected on schoolies to 28 inches both nights, with one better fish that spit the hook right at the rock. The pattern's consistent: bass are stacking on structure — the ledges from Castle Hill down through Brenton, the rock piles off Beavertail on the Jamestown side — and feeding hard right around the bottom of the tide when current compresses bait against the rock. Daytime, they've gone quiet on the open shore, but Sakonnet Point is still producing on the outgoing, especially the rip that forms off the point itself where the river current meets the open water. Sandeels and small bucktails, white or olive, worked slow along bottom in eight to fifteen feet, have been picking off keeper-class fish there on the last two hours of ebb.

Fluke have been the more reliable daytime play. The Sakonnet River, particularly the drift from the Stone Bridge area down past the old railroad trestle, has been giving up decent numbers on the incoming — four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, dragged slow over the mixed sand-and-mussel bottom in eighteen to twenty-two feet. Nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with the occasional four-pounder mixed in, but steady enough to keep rods bent. Point Judith and the mouth of the Narrow River are producing similarly — same depth range, same slow-drag presentation, best on the top half of the incoming when there's enough push to keep the boat moving but not so much you're bouncing bottom too fast to feel the bite.

Scup are about the easiest thing going right now, and I mean that as a compliment — if you've got kids or a buddy who just wants bent rods, the Newport Bridge pilings and the ledges around Jamestown are loaded. Squid strips or clam on a simple high-low rig, twenty to thirty feet, any stage of the tide really, though the slack periods make it easiest to keep bait down where they're holding.

Tog, I'll be honest with you, has been tough. The ledges off Beavertail and out toward Whale Rock still have fish on them — I marked good concentrations dropping green crabs down in eighteen to twenty-five feet last week — but the bite in this warm water is sluggish. You'll get the soft pickup, the slow mouthing, and then nothing. It's not a dead bite, it's a lazy one. My advice right now is don't burn a whole trip on tog — mix it into a day where you're also working bass or fluke, because the real tog window opens back up as the water starts cooling into September, and that's when these same ledges turn from stingy to stacked.

No albies yet, and I wouldn't tell you otherwise. That first push into the breachways — Weekapaug, the Charlestown breachway, Napatree — is still weeks off. What I am watching is the bait. If these peanut bunker schools stick around and thicken up through August the way they're trending, and the water temps ease back a touch off their summer peak, we could see an earlier-than-usual push into Napatree and the Sakonnet mouth come late August. That's a bigger if than a guarantee, but it's the kind of bait signal that's worth filing away.

For this coming week, if I've got one morning to give it, I'm back on the Ocean Drive ledges working the last two hours of the ebb into first light, betting the bass stay locked into that dark-water pattern until we get a real cooldown. Daytime, I'd rather be drifting the Sakonnet for fluke than standing on a hot rock hoping a tog decides to commit. Wind's been manageable out of the south-southwest most afternoons, which keeps the south-facing beaches fishable but chums up a little surface chop by early afternoon — plan around it, fish the mornings when you can.
